assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED is the architecture that made superconducting artificial atoms controllable and readable through microwave resonators: strong coupling, dispersive readout, and the cavity bus for multi-qubit gates. It is the foundation of essentially all superconducting quantum processors and of waveguide and microwave quantum optics on a chip. The idea is original (an on-chip analogue of cavity QED), clear, and has had very wide impact.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) are the decisive pieces. A three-person prize naturally pairs the experimental demonstration with the Yale theory and experiment leadership; Wallraff, Schoelkopf and Girvin are my reading of the core, but Blais has a strong theory claim and the fourth slot is genuinely contested.
assessment.maturity: Strong and independent confirmation in many groups worldwide over two decades, and a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely, with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits now establishing the context, though that prize is distinct in content and in laureates.
uncertainties: Whether Blais or Girvin should hold the theory slot is unresolved; with four credited names one is necessarily omitted.
Overlap in subject area with the 2025 prize could be read as too soon after it; I regard the discoveries as distinct.
I should disclose my own field proximity to circuit QED and treat that as a possible bias; I have not verified exact priority details beyond my recollection.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, with the magic-wavelength idea and strontium lattice demonstrations, have taken timekeeping to the 10^-18 level, opening tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a prospective redefinition of the second. The importance, clarity and measurable lasting impact are exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept (2001-2003) and demonstrated early clocks. Ye led the JILA realisation with record accuracy and stability. This is a clean two-person attribution; other contributors (for example Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) are credited at the working level but are not in the supplied names. Katori and Ye are the natural pair.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: many independent labs, repeated improvements, and international metrology agreement. Ye's earlier work is adjacent to the 2005 frequency-comb prize, but the clock concept is distinct. Timing is good.
uncertainties: Ye's prior ties to the 2005 comb work might raise a question of overlapping recognition, though the lattice clock is a separate invention.
Other ion-clock pioneers are not part of this candidate, so field-level credit remains partial.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum computing with trapped ions (1995) provided the first realistic physical blueprint for gates and a template for quantum simulation with atoms, with broad influence on AMO quantum information. It is original and conceptually clear.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the decisive joint authors of the proposal and of the subsequent theoretical framework for trapped-ion and atomic simulators. The credit is compact and unambiguous. Experimental realisation by Wineland's and Blatt's groups is outside this candidate, and Wineland's prize (2012) is already given.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed by ion-trap gates and quantum simulators, with trapped-ion machines now commercial. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: A prize may be seen as partly overlapping the 2012 prize for ion control, which could weaken the argument for novelty.
The role of the proposal relative to the experimental demonstrations that made it influential needs careful wording.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity opened the field of moire quantum matter, with a very large experimental and theoretical literature. Originality and impact are high, and it connects naturally to superconducting physics.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 continuum-model prediction of the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group reported the 2018 correlated insulator and superconductivity. That is a natural theory plus experiment trio. The contributions of Cory Dean and others on moire systems and of the Harvard and Columbia groups are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Rapid replication across many groups, but the origin of superconductivity and correlated states is still debated. Timing is plausible but some elements of the interpretation remain open.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene is not settled.
Whether moire physics broadly, rather than one material, is the proper prize unit is unclear.
The experimental credit may need to include other groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, followed by experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, established topological insulators as a new class of quantum matter. It is original, conceptually clean, and broadly influential, including links to Majorana physics and topological quantum computation.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical contributions; Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental observation (with the Zhang group's HgTe prediction, which is not in the supplied names). Hasan has a strong claim on three-dimensional topological insulator observation with ARPES, which makes the optimal three-name configuration contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently in several materials and by many experiments; the interpretation is stable. Recognition is mature and arguably due.
uncertainties: Priority issues for the HgTe prediction (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) and the 3D case (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hasan) make a clean split difficult.
The two-dimensional and three-dimensional discoveries may need separate recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned the foundations of quantum mechanics into a practical information-theoretically secure primitive and helped start quantum information science. The idea is original and has lasting conceptual and technological impact.
assessment.attribution: BB84 (Bennett and Brassard) and the entanglement-based Ekert protocol are the principal contributions; this triple represents the field's recognised founders, though Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not among the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations, fibre and satellite links and commercial systems confirm the concept; security proofs have matured but practical implementation security is still evolving. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Wiesner's priority (conjugate coding) is not representable with the given names.
Part of the impact lies in information science and engineering rather than physics discovery per se.
Partial overlap with the 2022 prize on entanglement experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and the threshold theorem underpin all scalable quantum computing, and Kitaev's topological approach underlies surface-code architectures. As a scientist working on error-corrected processors I regard this as foundational, although it is largely theoretical and mathematical.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane introduced the first codes, Kitaev the toric code and anyonic fault tolerance; the threshold results involved others (Aharonov, Ben-Or, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill, Gottesman) not credited here. A three-name set captures the central ideas but leaves out notable contributors.
assessment.maturity: Recent experiments show error suppression below threshold with surface codes, supporting the theory, but a full fault-tolerant machine is not yet demonstrated. Recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across many people and the three-name selection is somewhat arbitrary.
Large-scale validation of fault tolerance is still pending, so maturity is incomplete.
Whether this is physics rather than computer science or mathematics for the prize is debatable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Anyonic statistics for particles in two dimensions is a deep conceptual discovery, with fractional statistics now observed in the fractional quantum Hall regime and relevant for topological quantum computing. The importance is high if experimental evidence is considered conclusive.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim (1977) made the original prediction; Wilczek and Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek contributions are not in the supplied names. On the experimental side, Heiblum (and Fève, Manfra) led the interferometry and collider experiments, a source of attribution uncertainty.
assessment.maturity: Collider and interferometer experiments in 2020 onward are recent and still being scrutinised. Non-Abelian anyons are not established. Recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Missing Wilczek from the names weakens a theory-credit configuration.
Interpretation of interferometry experiments continues to be refined.
The experimental subgroup of six names makes a fair split difficult.
